headline.main: Pankaj Mishra on the War in Gaza: "Germany's Reputation Has Been Badly Tainted by its One-Sided Support for the Israeli Government"
headline.social: Pankaj Mishra on the War in Gaza: Germany's Reputation Has Been Badly Tainted by its One-Sided Support for the Israeli Government"

intro: In his new book, "The World After Gaza," Indian author Pankaj Mishra is sharply critical of Western support for Israel's war in Gaza. He is particularly disapproving of German politics and memory culture.
text:
DER SPIEGEL: Mr. Mishra, you grew up in India. You have written that a picture of Moshe Dayan, the Israeli defense minister from 1967 to 1974, was hanging in your childhood bedroom. What about this man with the famous eye patch did you find so impressive?
Mishra: He represented Israeli military efficiency and a cult of heroism. People in my family felt that we didn’t have a coherent sense of nationality in India, that we didn't believe in our nation strongly enough. We knew very little about the state of Israel, about the history of Zionism and the persecution of Jews in Europe. But we had the impression that people like Moshe Dayan had created a very strong state and a very cohesive society. We saw Israel as a model from which we in India could learn and benefit.
DER SPIEGEL: Do people in the Global South, who have often experienced racism and persecution themselves, have a better understanding of the Middle East conflict? Do they feel more empathy – with both sides?
Mishra: The nationalist leaders of India and China felt deep sympathy for the European Jews, who were so viciously persecuted. The idea that they were entitled to their own country was well received at the time in Asia, and also in Africa. This changed after 1948, when Israel came into being and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were expelled and dispossessed. That is when the sympathy switched sides.
DER SPIEGEL: You also expressed understanding for the fact that Jews "must have a state of their own and should never be reduced to a minority.” Now, you have written a book that is scathingly critical of Israel and its supporters. When did your own sympathy switch sides?
Mishra: The people who founded the state of Israel out of a very urgent and grave historical necessity had an absolute right to their own nation state. This is also true of many peoples in Asia and Africa, who suffered decades of cruel European imperialism. But once these nation states came into existence, a different kind of history began. When the rulers of India, Israel, China and Indonesia began to treat their minorities or indigenous peoples the way they were once treated by their European tormentors, they lost whatever claim to virtue they might have had in the past. If you measure these states by the same moral and political standards as all other states, then it is not difficult to switch your sympathies to those who are now their victims.
DER SPIEGEL: Is the extermination of Jewish life on an industrial scale during the Holocaust in any way comparable to the crimes of colonialism and the oppression of minorities since?
Mishra: Who is comparing them? No country is authorized by the terrible suffering of previous generations to commit crimes against humanity in the present. Many Germans seem to think they have the right to give a moral license in perpetuity to Israel, no matter how extreme its government becomes. These Germans may continue to think so and remain prisoners of the past. But the rest of the world will have to judge both Germany and Israel by its actions in the present.
DER SPIEGEL: Your new book "The World After Gaza” traces more than a century of European, Jewish and Palestinian history and quotes hundreds of authors. But you mention Hamas, the events of October 7, 2023, and the victims in Israel and Gaza only in passing. Why is that?
Mishra: I’m not obsessed with Hamas in the way one is expected to be. You are constantly asked by the defenders of Israel: Why do you not speak about Hamas, this militant organization that threatens to wipe Israel off the map?
DER SPIEGEL: Doesn't it do that?
Mishra: It has also agreed to a two-state solution. Why do we want to suppress that fact? In the history of anti-colonialism, there have been many movements which were once described as terrorist – most prominently the African National Congress, whose former leader Nelson Mandela was officially classified as a terrorist by the U.S. and most Western European countries until 2008.
DER SPIEGEL: Are you comparing Hamas with the ANC?
Mishra: The atrocities of October 7 pale into insignificance when compared to the atrocities committed by Indian men against European women and children during the Indian Mutiny of 1857. The people who committed those crimes are now being hailed as freedom fighters, and statues have been erected to them all over India.
DER SPIEGEL: What are you getting at? Those events in India took place almost 200 years ago. And the ANC never committed a massacre like Hamas.
Mishra: I’m making a very different argument. If you look at history from the perspective of Western or white supremacy, anyone who resists is automatically denounced as a savage terrorist. But can things be so simple? In the history of anti-colonial movements, there has often been extreme violence, from India’s first freedom fighters and anti-French Algerians to the Palestine Liberation Organization, the PLO. You have to look at the eruptions of violence by non-state actors in their political and historical context of continuous state violence. I condemn Hamas’ atrocities, but I am not going to separate October 7, 2023, from the long history of people rising up ferociously and brutally against their longstanding oppressors.
DER SPIEGEL: You have said that your book is a response to the attempt by Western politicians and journalists to conceal not only the extent of the Israeli offensive in Gaza, but also the history of the Israeli occupation. But many governments, from Norway to Spain, from South Africa to Brazil, have spoken out clearly about the suffering of the Palestinian people and many media outlets have reported on it extensively.
Mishra: Are you suggesting that the European and American media have covered the atrocities inflicted by Israel on Gaza with the same granular detail as the atrocities committed by Hamas on October 7?
DER SPIEGEL: As far as DER SPIEGEL is concerned, I strongly disagree with your insinuation. We have reported in great detail and with great accuracy on the carnage in Gaza and the victims on the Palestinian side. This also applies to many other media.
Mishra: The destruction of Gaza has been documented mainly by Palestinian journalists, and many of them have been killed by the Israeli army. It would be a grave distortion of the truth to claim that the suffering of the Palestinians is being adequately reported by the Western press. Especially since October 7, we’ve seen an incredible inequality of compassion and attention between Israeli and Palestinian victims. This has been shocking for most people around the world.
DER SPIEGEL: You accuse Western politicians of not just covering up the realities of the Israeli offensive, but also Israel’s expansion into the West Bank and the destruction of peaceful Palestinian movements. Are you implying an international conspiracy?
Mishra: I am not implying any conspiracy whatsoever. Nations like South Africa, Brazil and Bolivia, and also European countries such as Spain, Ireland and Slovenia, have insisted that international law be observed in Israel’s assault on Hamas. Israel had every right to take action against Hamas after the attacks on October 7. But there are certain laws that every state must abide by. And when Spain and Ireland concluded that these laws were not being observed, they called on the other European countries to impose sanctions. These appeals were actively ignored, including by the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.
DER SPIEGEL: You are particularly critical of German politics. You write that the country has become "complicit ... in murderous ethno-nationalism” through its "unconditional solidarity” with the Israeli government. Is it not understandable that Germany instinctively sided with Israel after October 7 given its history?
Mishra: It wasn't just the Germans who sided with Israel. Most people around the world were absolutely appalled by the war crimes committed on October 7. Very few would have questioned Israel's right to go after those responsible for the murder of hundreds of civilians. And if Israel had acted responsibly, world sympathy would have remained on Israel's side. But if I have read the surveys correctly, many Germans said that a ceasefire was necessary very early on in this war - an opinion that was consistently ignored by politicians. Of course Germany has a historical responsibility towards Israel. But does this give the Israeli government endless license to carry out such unprecedented massacres in Gaza? Shouldn’t Germany's responsibility convert into a deeper responsibility to end this violence?
DER SPIEGEL: "I privately recoiled,” you write, "when friends and acquaintances in the media grew rancorous in their criticisms of Israel, blaming their inability to express them publicly on Jews in prominent positions." Do you share the concerns that many have about a resurgence of anti-Semitism?
Mishra: When you hear conspiracy theories about Jews being in powerful positions and so on, all alarm bells go off. Antisemitism is a very powerful force. It can never be underestimated. But those who claim to be virtuous by invoking an experience of victimhood, especially one that they have not suffered themselves, should not be taken at face value. Especially not a nation state that turns down chances of peace with its neighbors and continues stealing and brutally occupying the lands of people it has displaced. And the rest of us, including the Germans, no matter what their history has been, have to be free, have to be morally liberated from the past to say that this is wrong.
DER SPIEGEL: You once praised Germany as the only country whose political culture is based on being aware of the disaster it has brought upon the world. Do you think differently today?
Mishra: I'm not the only one here. I join a lot of people around the world who have been forced to reexamine their attachment to, indeed their admiration for, Germany’s memory culture. As I wrote in a DER SPIEGEL essay two years ago, Germany had an incredible opportunity to create a new bridge to the countries of Asia and Africa and help create the new structures and institutions we need to confront challenges that are global and not merely national or regional in nature. Compared to other European nations, the impact of German colonialism in Asia was minimal. A lot of people in India or Indonesia don't even know about Germany's colonialism. But Germany committed itself to an idea of the West that is falling apart before our eyes today.
DER SPIEGEL: In what respect?
Mishra: Look at the trajectory the United States has taken. The U.S. president is threatening Denmark, a NATO country, and we hardly hear a peep from Europe. Germany has to recalibrate its choices and its place in the wider world. The German elites don't want to hear this because they have been too invested in this alliance with the United States and too accustomed to thinking that NATO is eternal. At the same time, in large parts of Asia and Africa, Germany's reputation has been badly tainted because of its one-sided support for the Israeli government. This is a terrible situation to be in for a country that only a few months ago was held in such high regard around the world. I cannot think of any other historical example of a country that possessed such an enormous amount of soft power and destroyed it in such short time.
DER SPIEGEL: Is that fair? Germany has been one of the largest humanitarian donors in the Palestinian Territories for decades. You yourself quote Helmut Schmidt, who clashed with Israel's Prime Minister Menachem Begin in 1981 when he said that Germany also had a moral responsibility towards the Palestinians.
Mishra: It’s baffling how that early sympathy for the Palestinians expressed by Helmut Schmidt and Willy Brandt has disappeared. When I went to Germany for the first time in the late 1990s, I came across a much more cosmopolitan, much broader view of the world. But Germany has changed, and now an explicitly far-right party is likely to emerge as the second strongest party in the Bundestag elections. I am as baffled by this as many others.
DER SPIEGEL: "The political and moral deformations and intellectual helplessness of Germany today," you write, "are more dangerous than at any other time since 1945." What do you mean by that?
Mishra: Perhaps the greatest failure of Germany’s memory culture is not its support for Israel or its blindness to the eradication of Gaza. It is the rise of this party that has been classified by Germany's own intelligence organizations as extremist, even fascist in parts. The fact that politicians from the center-right CDU are even contemplating working with this party at federal level is an extraordinary repudiation of Germany’s memory culture.
DER SPIEGEL: What does this have to do with Israel?
Mishra: The U.S. and Germany are the biggest contributors to the Israeli military arsenal. In both cases, the blind support for Israel has been followed by a surging far right. This signals a dramatic change in political mentality. We are increasingly dealing with a culture in which laws, morality and ordinary decency are no longer cherished and falsity, deception and hypocrisy have become the norm. And it’s in those political circumstances that the far right triumphs.
DER SPIEGEL: Do you really see a causal link between Germany’s support of Israel and the rise of the AfD?
Mishra: German readers would understand better than most people the insidious dynamic of nihilism. There are whole libraries out there about how the unprecedented violence and mass destruction of World War I helped accelerate the rise of the far right in Europe. Remember what George Orwell, Arthur Koestler and many others said of the Spanish Civil War. German bombs destroyed the city of Guernica – a harbinger of continent-wide total war and destruction. Today, Germany is supporting what organizations like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch call a genocide. Do you really think that Germany can remain unaffected by the wildfire spreading from this bonfire of international law and morality?
DER SPIEGEL: German Chancellor Olaf Scholz has read your books. Have you ever spoken to him, or would you be interested in doing so?
Mishra: Before October 7, 2023, I was due to visit Germany and meet with legislators of the Green Party. Then the attack happened, and I said that if I do appear in public with Green Party members, I will have to make clear my own positions on this issue. It was communicated to me that that would be quite impossible. So I canceled my trip to Germany and I have not been there since. I am always open to discussing different views on the state of the world. But at this stage, I am at risk of losing my own credibility by appearing with politicians who have been complicit in these monstrous acts of violence in Gaza.
DER SPIEGEL: You criticize the hypocrisy of the West when it comes to the Middle East conflict. But you are relatively measured in your criticism of the countries of the Global South. In the Arab world, the events of October 7 are still being denied by some to this day. Isn't hypocrisy fairly evenly distributed between the West and the South?
Mishra: I subscribe to that last sentence. But I very strongly object to the idea that I’ve been lenient with the countries of the Global South. I have been extremely critical of the Indian regimes, not just under Narendra Modi. I have written about Tibet, about China's treatment of protesters in Hong Kong, about Indonesia’s and Myanmar's treatment of their minorities. Indian readers who follow my writings and dislike them make the claim that I never criticize Germany, America or Britain the way I criticize India. I think they are right. I am relentlessly harsh in my criticism of the Indian treatment of its Muslim and Christian minorities.
DER SPIEGEL: And the Arab countries?
Mishra: I have also been critical of the Arab states that I have traveled to. But I’m not going to criticize them simply to balance my criticism of Israel. I can guarantee you one thing, however: If a Palestinian state were to come into existence and became oppressive to its minorities or started to threaten Israel's existence, then I know what I would be doing then – and where my sympathies would lie.
DER SPIEGEL: The epilogue of your book is entitled "Hope in a Dark Time.” Is it possible that the suffering on both sides and the global shock that this war has triggered might lead to a moral reconsideration?
Mishra: I'm afraid that would be too optimistic. My hope is much more modest. The young people who have been exposed to these atrocities and have seen people of our generation enabling or condoning them have been shocked into moral adulthood. I hope that one day they will create a world in which such misery is at least no longer sanctioned. Given the way things are going in the United States and in large parts of Western Europe, we cannot really hope for a political or moral recovery of the kind we saw after 1945. We are definitely heading for dark times. But we do have one generation that is morally awake.
DER SPIEGEL: Mr. Mishra, thank you very much for this interview.
